subject: Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?

messages.author: 04e62c3b36bb17bf
messages.subject: Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?
parts:
Hi Karl et al,
I am working with expression phenotypes- lots of them (>20,000).
For many of these, the appropriate model is 2part, because there are many 0 counts. I am trying apply the same pipeline to all phenotypes - 10k scantwo perms, stepwise model selection, output various stats. So, instead of running 2part, which cannot be fit in scantwo/stepwiseQTL, I am planning on running two rounds, one normal (excluding the 0 count phenotypes) and one binary (all 0-counts set to 0 and all others set to 1).

Here's the problem: scantwo perms for model = "binary" is extremely slow. So slow that it is not feasible to run on a 24 cluster 48gb node on our server, even for a single phenotype, let alone 20,000. The other analyses are relatively fast, even with model = binary. So, I am looking for a way around running the scantwo permutations. 

Here's my thought process: For binary traits, there should be some global permutation levels that apply to all traits, no matter the study (right?). Kind of like taking a single set of permutations for a dataset of quantile normalized phenotypes. If that is the case, the n(0)/n(1) for a given binary phenotype should always return a single, exact permutation threshold. Therefore we could predict the permutation thresholds for any binary phenotype by the ratio of 0's:1's using a non-linear (or linear) regression. 

Solutions?: 
1) Is there an easy way to speed up the model = "binary" scantwos? I imagine not, but if so, great!
2) If not, what if we got our hands on a huge node >= 1tb and ran 10k perms for 10 sets of binary phenotypes with 0/1 ratios of .05, .1, .15, .20, .25, .30, .35, .40, .45, .50. Would it be statistically sound to then fit a model and predict the thresholds at all 0/1 ratios and use those for each gene expression phenotype? If so, we could then get around running 20k sets of perms with just 10.
Thoughts?
Thanks for all of the help!
John

John T. Lovell, Ph.D.
Postdoctoral Fellow
Department of Integrative Biology
University of Texas, Austin

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?
parts:
The binary trait analysis is slower than that for a regular quantitative trait because it uses an iterative algorithm to fit a logistic regression model. So at each pair of locations, a series of regressions will be fit, instead of just one.

I like your solution (2). You might want to use more ratios at the low end than the high end...perhaps something like 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.16, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5.

You might also play with reducing the number of iterations in the fit. You might even want to go into the C code and change the stopping rule. (I'm thinking that, for the purpose of permutations, one would want to stop early if the LOD score is not big, and go longer only if there's evidence that the LOD score is going to be largish.)

Regards,
karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?
parts:
Hi Karl,
Thanks for the response. 
I am working on implementing model = "binary" in my QTL pipeline and am running into some issues with convergence. 
I sometimes receive an error from stepwiseqtl:
"In fitqtlengine(pheno = pheno, qtl = qtl, covar = covar, formula = formula,  : Didn't converge."
In this case, scanone converges, but stepwiseqtl doesn't (I think the error is generated from refineqtl, but I am not sure). 

For one of these error producing phenotypes, I did some troubleshooting-  the algorithm doesn't converge until the tolerance is increased to 0.2 (up from 0.0001).Changing the number of iterations does not seem to effect the threshold of convergence (I have tried 4k,10k, 100k and 1M iterations). 

Do you have any thoughts on what might be constraining the convergence and how I can increase the probability of convergence without increasing the tolerance?
Thanks,
John

messages.author: d5fdb09d679f8c32
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?
parts:
John,

It might be due to low counts when you cross-tabulate the binary phenotype with all the QTL in your model.  This happens in logistic regression if you have too many variables in your model or if they are collinear or if the binary phenotype is has low frequency.

- Decrease the number of QTL you consider
- Decrease number of linked or interacting QTL

Failing these, add a small amount of noise (with variance 0.01) to the phenotype and treat the data as normal.

Other solutions to consider would involve tacking the numerical algorithm directly.

Saunak

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?
parts:
Thanks Saunak! 
I think you are right; I typically am getting errors from samples that have only a few observations in one cell of the test. Not sure how I'll be able to get around that in my current experimental design while using model = "binary". 
So, have you explored the performance of adding variance to binary traits and fitting them as normal? If this approach is robust, it could dramatically speed up my pipeline. Here is a comparison of the binary model and the normal model, fit to the data with sd = 0.01 around 0 or 1 for the 1st 5 of my binary traits: 
https://johntlovell.files.wordpress.com/2014/10/binary-normal-comps.pdf 
Basically, when the binary model converges, we get nearly identical scanone profiles, with the normal model fitting slightly better. When the binary model does not converge, we get much better fits from the normal model.
Thoughts?
John

messages.author: d5fdb09d679f8c32
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?
parts:
The normal noise-added model I suggested is a hack, and is intended as a way to get out of the numerical convergence issue.  A genome scan is basically a regression model multiplexed.  In your case, logistic regression is having numerical problems because of sparse counts.  There is something called "exact logistic regression" that is meant for this scenario.  SAS and Stata have implementations, but R only has an approximate version as far as I know.  But using exact logistic regression is not a realistic option, I would think.

If you are using permutation testing, then you can use the noise-added hack to make your pipeline go through.  Make sure that your final conclusions are not too dependent on this choice, however, when you get the final results.  For example, if you end up getting a hit with sparse counts, you should be suspicious.

Saunak

Mehta, Cyrus R. and Patel, Nitin R. (1995), “Exact Logistic Regression: Theory and Examples,” Statistics in Medicine, 14, 2143–2160
